t.2.25.1: To Sītā, who was speaking thus, he who knew dharma, who cherished dharma, and whose very self was dharma, spoke these words for the purpose of turning her back.
t.2.25.3: O Sītā, O delicate one, as I shall tell you, so must you act. For in the forest there are many dangers; learn of them from me as I speak.
t.2.25.2: Sītā, you are of a very noble family and always devoted to dharma. Practise your own dharma here, and treat me in the way that brings happiness to my mind.
t.2.25.4: Sītā, let this resolve you have made to dwell in the forest be abandoned, for the forest is said to be a wilderness full of dangers.
t.2.25.5: Indeed, these words are spoken by me out of concern for your welfare. I do not know the forest to be ever pleasant; the forest is always nothing but hardship.
t.2.25.6: The roars of the lions that dwell in mountain caves, mingled with the sound of mountain waterfalls, are painful to hear; therefore the forest is a place of hardship.
t.2.25.7: At night, worn out with toil, one must sleep on the bare ground upon beds of leaves that one has broken off oneself; therefore the forest is full of hardship.
t.2.25.8: Fasting must be undertaken, O Maithilī, as far as one's strength allows, and a mass of matted locks must be borne by one who wears garments of bark.
t.2.25.9: Here there is fierce wind, darkness, and constant hunger, and here too are great dangers; therefore the forest is a place of greater sorrow.
t.2.25.10: And many serpents of many forms, O passionate lady, roam the earth in their arrogance; therefore the forest is even more full of hardship.
t.2.25.11: Serpents that dwell in rivers, moving crookedly like rivers, lie coiled across the path; therefore the forest is a place of great hardship.
t.2.25.12: Flying insects, scorpions, worms and gadflies, together with mosquitoes, constantly torment one, O weak woman; therefore the forest is wholly full of suffering.
t.2.25.13: In the forest there are thorny trees, and kuśa and kāśa grasses, O passionate lady, with the tips of their branches tangled every which way; therefore the forest is a place of great hardship.
t.2.25.14: Therefore, enough of your going to the forest, for the forest is not fit for you. Reflecting on it here, I see the forest as fraught with ever greater dangers.
t.2.25.15: When the great-souled Rāma did not make up his mind to take her to the forest, Sītā did not accept those words of his; then, deeply distressed, she spoke this to Rāma.
